name: Digital Euro Regulation
evidence_rating: ex-ante only: Commission IA and ECB simulations, contested industry cost study; regulation not adopted
summary: The Commission judged that a digital euro's benefits outweigh set-up costs of several billion euros if holding limits protect banks. ECB simulations suggest a EUR 3,000 limit would leave bank funding largely unaffected in normal times, though a severe crisis could shift up to EUR 699 billion of deposits; a bank-funded study puts banks' costs at EUR 18 billion or more, well above ECB estimates. The law is still being negotiated, so there is no evidence of actual effects.

indicators.objective: No LFS indicators section; the memorandum names monitoring indicators and requires a Commission review three years after application and every three years thereafter
Use of central bank money in digital payments
indicators.indicator: Amount of digital euro in circulation; number and value of retail payments in digital euro and share vs other means of payment
indicators.evidence: Not applicable: regulation not adopted (Council position Dec 2025; Parliament mandate 2026; ECB targets issuance around 2029).

indicators.indicator: Holding limits keep deposit substitution manageable
indicators.target_or_baseline: ECB: a EUR 3,000 holding limit caps supply at max ~EUR 1tn
indicators.evidence: Ex-ante simulations only: ECB (2025) estimates flight-to-safety outflows of EUR 156bn (EUR 500 limit) to EUR 699bn (EUR 3,000 limit; 8.2% of retail sight deposits); contained in business-as-usual.

indicators.indicator: One-off costs for PSPs and merchants
indicators.target_or_baseline: PSPs up to EUR 3.6-6.8bn; merchants already accepting cards EUR 0.8-14bn
indicators.evidence: Contested ex-ante: bank-commissioned PwC study puts bank costs at ~EUR 18bn over four years; ECB counters with ~EUR 4-5.8bn (per secondary reports).

literature.citation: European Commission (2023), Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals on the establishment of the digital euro and on digital euro services, SWD(2023) 233 (executive summary SWD(2023) 234)
literature.title: Impact Assessment accompanying the proposals on the establishment of the digital euro and on digital euro services
literature.outcomes: financial stability; payment choice; strategic autonomy; costs
literature.headline: Long-term benefits judged to outweigh costs; holding limits to protect financial stability (citing ECB: EUR 3,000 limit caps supply at max EUR 1tn; JRC bank-by-bank analysis). One-off costs: PSPs up to EUR 6.8bn (or EUR 3.6bn with size-differentiated method); merchants already accepting e-payments EUR 0.8-14bn; recurring costs not estimated
literature.summary_plain: The Commission judged that a digital euro's long-term benefits - payment choice, a public anchor for money and less reliance on foreign card schemes - outweigh set-up costs of several billion euros, provided holding limits protect banks.
literature.verified: executive summary read; full text searched

literature.citation: Adalid, Álvarez-Blázquez, Assenmacher et al. (2022), Central bank digital currency and bank intermediation, ECB Occasional Paper No 293
literature.title: Central bank digital currency and bank intermediation
literature.headline: Illustrative take-up scenarios from just under EUR 500bn to just over EUR 7tn; effects on bank intermediation vary across banks in normal times and are potentially larger in stress; impact on bank-run dynamics depends on remuneration and usage limits
literature.summary_plain: ECB staff simulations found a digital euro's effect on bank funding would differ a lot between banks and could be bigger in a crisis, which is why holding limits matter.
literature.quality: ECB staff simulation; views of authors
literature.interested_party: ECB is the prospective issuer of the digital euro

literature.citation: European Central Bank (2025), Technical data on the financial stability impact of the digital euro, ECB technical annex for co-legislators, 10 October 2025
literature.title: Technical data on the financial stability impact of the digital euro
literature.venue: ECB technical annex for co-legislators, 10 October 2025
literature.method: simulation (supervisory deposit data, business-as-usual and flight-to-safety scenarios)
literature.headline: Business-as-usual: deposit impact contained for all limits up to EUR 3,000; net interest income falls 9-18bp (without digitalisation trend). Flight-to-safety: outflows EUR 156bn (EUR 500 limit) to EUR 699bn (EUR 3,000; 2.2% of bank assets, 8.2% of retail sight deposits); at EUR 3,000, 13 banks (0.3% of assets) reach 100% LCR and 9 (0.1%) could fall below
literature.summary_plain: The ECB estimates that with a EUR 3,000 holding limit, a severe crisis could move up to EUR 699 billion of deposits into digital euros, but only a handful of small banks would run short of liquidity; in normal times the effect is small.
literature.quality: illustrative; ECB says not its full methodology
literature.interested_party: ECB is the prospective issuer of the digital euro

literature.citation: PwC (for EACB, EBF and ESBG) (2025), Digital Euro Cost Study, Study commissioned by European bank associations, June 2025
literature.title: Digital Euro Cost Study
literature.venue: Study commissioned by European bank associations, June 2025
literature.method: survey of 19 euro-area retail banks, extrapolated
literature.headline: Change costs of over EUR 2bn for 19 surveyed banks; extrapolated EUR 18-30bn across the euro area over the first four years (average ~EUR 110m per bank); ECB later put initial investment at roughly EUR 4-5.8bn
literature.summary_plain: A study paid for by bank associations estimated the digital euro would cost euro-area banks about EUR 18 billion or more to introduce, far above the ECB's own estimate.
literature.interested_party: Commissioned by bank associations (EACB, EBF, ESBG) opposed to current design
